hook: If your anxiety spikes the moment you get into bed — there's a neurological reason that happens at exactly that time.
body:
**If your anxiety spikes the moment you get into bed — there's a neurological reason that happens at exactly that time.**

During the day, your brain has continuous input to process — tasks, conversations, screens, movement. That input occupies the prefrontal cortex. It doesn't eliminate the anxiety signal, but it competes with it.

The moment you lie down, the input stops. The signal doesn't. It was always there. You've just removed everything that was covering it.

There's also a cortisol component. Your body has a natural cortisol dip in the late evening that paradoxically lowers your stress threshold — meaning things that felt manageable at 3pm can feel genuinely threatening at 11pm. This isn't your imagination. It's your hormone cycle.

So the anxious thoughts that flood in at night aren't new problems. They're old signals with nowhere left to hide.

What works here isn't forcing yourself to sleep. It's giving your nervous system a deliberate wind-down signal before you lie down — not after.

The pre-sleep protocol is in the free guide in my bio.
